The WebSocket first frame for the forged token was {"type":"welcome","playerId":"a8855df0-c18d-4b75-b498-89f62b6fe1e2","displayName":"Mallory","onlinePlayers":1}. The control-token WebSocket handshake was refused. Not exercised: the AI routes (AI_PROVIDER=none) and full battle submit/report as the victim. Those effects come from source only.

remediation.strategy: Stop shipping a secret value that passes validation. Leave JWT_SECRET empty in .env.example, which makes the server generate a random secret and log a warning. In Config.fromEnv, reject known placeholders and obviously low-entropy values. Optionally add a compose guard (e.g. JWT_SECRET: ${JWT_SECRET:?Set JWT_SECRET}) together with the code check. Regression test: AppConfig.fromEnv(mapOf("JWT_SECRET" to "replace-with-a-long-random-secret-at-least-32-chars")) must throw, and so must fromEnv(mapOf("JWT_SECRET" to "a".repeat(32))).

code_changes.fixed_code:
# HS256 signing secret, at least 32 random characters: openssl rand -base64 48
# The server refuses example values. Leave empty only for throwaway local runs (random per-process secret).
JWT_SECRET=

likelihood.reason: An operator has to skip replacing one placeholder line after the documented copy step, even though three comments tell them to replace it. When they do skip it, nothing stops or warns them: the server logs jwtSecret=provided, and compose guards only that DB_PASSWORD is present.

impact.reason: Full impersonation of any existing player across all authenticated APIs: battle as the victim, file reports as the victim, earn or lose wins, and use up the victim's AI rate-limit quota. It also allows an unvalidated display name that is broadcast to co-players and stored in battle results. There are no admin roles, no cross-player data beyond game state, and no way to create new identities through this path.

confidence.reason: The full source trace was checked line by line, and an independent sandboxed run of the real server main reproduced the result. The placeholder was accepted, the control token was rejected, a forged token for a nonexistent subject was rejected, and the forged victim token authenticated on both HTTP and WebSocket.

title: Registration rate limit becomes one global bucket behind the recommended reverse proxy
description: The anonymous POST /v1/auth/register route is wrapped in RATE_LIMIT_REGISTER, which allows 10 requests per 60 s. Its bucket key is call.request.origin.remoteHost. The server installs no XForwardedHeaders or ForwardedHeaders plugin and has no trusted-proxy setting, so the key is always the immediate TCP peer and forwarded headers are ignored. The backend README (line 108) tells operators to run the server behind a TLS reverse proxy. In that topology every client reaches Netty from the proxy's address. One anonymous client sending 10 registrations a minute would then get 429 rate_limited returned to every other new user of the instance, which blocks account creation and therefore all online features for newcomers. I reproduced the mechanism independently in the sandbox with a simulated proxy. A real client sent 10 registrations through a loopback relay that forwards the client address in X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP and Forwarded, and all 10 got 201. A different real client's first request through the same relay then got 429. Direct peers kept separate buckets: A got 429 on its 11th request while B and E got 201. The shipped docker-compose publishes 8080 directly and has no proxy service, so whether a deployment actually puts an address-replacing hop in front is not visible in source.
claimed_root_cause: The register limiter uses the TCP peer address as the client identity (Application.kt:159, requestKey { call.request.origin.remoteHost }). The plugin set installed in lexiFlowModule (Application.kt:152-161 and surrounding installs) has no XForwardedHeaders/ForwardedHeaders plugin, and Config.fromEnv has no trusted-proxy option. Meanwhile the documented deployment (README.md:108) puts a reverse proxy in front of the server. rateLimitRegisterPerMinute is fixed at its default of 10 (Config.kt:42), and fromEnv (Config.kt:60-103) sets only rateLimitAiPerMinute from the environment, so an operator cannot raise the limit by configuration either.

trace.description: Anonymous registration endpoint (no authentication), wrapped in rateLimit(RATE_LIMIT_REGISTER) at line 34.
rateLimiter(limit = config.rateLimitRegisterPerMinute (10), refillPeriod = 60 s).

The bucket key is call.request.origin.remoteHost. With no forwarded-header plugin this is the immediate TCP peer, which is the proxy for every proxied client, so all such clients share one 10/min bucket.

evidence.description: requestKey { call -> call.request.origin.remoteHost } is the only identity used by the register limiter.

install(RateLimit). The module imports and installs only ContentNegotiation, CallLogging, WebSockets, Authentication, RateLimit and StatusPages. It has no XForwardedHeaders/ForwardedHeaders and no trusted-proxy configuration (the imports at lines 22-55 contain no forwarded-header plugin).
The README tells operators to run the server behind TLS through a reverse proxy ('Sunucuyu TLS arkasında (reverse proxy) çalıştırın').

rateLimitRegisterPerMinute defaults to 10. Config.fromEnv (lines 60-103) sets only RATE_LIMIT_AI_PER_MINUTE (line 102) and exposes no register-limit or proxy-trust option. This corrects the hunter's citation of line 245, which does not exist because the file has 112 lines.
The shipped compose publishes ${HOST_PORT:-8080}:8080 directly and defines no proxy service. The topology actually in front of the server is therefore deployment-dependent.

blockers: Whether the production instance takes client connections through a reverse proxy, load balancer, CDN or Docker userland-proxy (for example IPv6, rootless Docker or Docker Desktop) that replaces the client source address is a deployment fact outside source. Locally I only showed that the key ignores forwarded headers and uses the TCP peer, and that a simulated address-replacing proxy makes all its clients share one bucket.

validation_plan.local: Done independently. The results are in agents/v3-11/artifacts/evidence-1.txt. The harness script is at agents/v3-11/scratch/evidence-2.txt and was not promoted to artifacts. The real server ran in the sandbox on loopback with a dummy JWT_SECRET and the in-memory store. Direct client A from 127.0.0.2 got 201 x10, then 429. Direct client B from 127.0.0.3 got 201, so buckets are per peer. A loopback relay at 127.0.0.1:18081 with upstream source 127.0.0.4 added X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP and Forwarded with the real client address. Client C from 127.0.0.5 got 201 x10 through it. Client D from 127.0.0.6 got 429 on its first request ever. Control client E, connecting directly from 127.0.0.7, got 201. The hunters' h-wild/h-deploy evidence agrees. Regression test to add after the fix: install XForwardedHeaders restricted to a configured trusted-proxy address and key on the derived client address. Then, through the trusted proxy hop, exhausting one forwarded client's 10/min bucket must not return 429 for a second forwarded client, and forwarded headers sent from an untrusted peer must still be ignored.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks their own staging deployment, not production traffic. Optionally, first add a temporary debug log of call.request.origin.remoteHost and confirm what the server sees for two different external client hosts; if both show the proxy or gateway IP, the condition holds. Then, within one minute, send 10 POST /v1/auth/register requests with dummy display names from client host A through the public URL, followed by one request from a different client host B. If B gets 429 rate_limited, the bucket is shared. Delete the dummy accounts afterwards.

title: Operator-paid AI budget escapes the per-player limit through free, unlimited identity minting
description: The only control on operator-paid Claude calls is a 20/min token bucket keyed on the JWT subject (Application.kt:154-155). Subjects are minted anonymously by POST /v1/auth/register (gated only by a 10/min per-remoteHost register limit, no proof of personhood), and each new token is valid for 90 days and immediately gets its own fresh 20/min AI budget. There is no per-source, global, daily or spend ceiling in Application.kt's install(RateLimit) block (only RATE_LIMIT_AI and RATE_LIMIT_REGISTER) or in Config.kt. One anonymous requester from a single source address can therefore grow its sustained AI throughput by ~200 calls/min for each minute spent registering (10 new identities/min x 20 calls/min each), against the operator's ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, with up to 2 billed provider calls per counted request (corrective retry). The result is unbounded operator spend, or exhaustion of the operator's shared provider quota so AI is denied to every legitimate player.
root_cause: RATE_LIMIT_AI accounts on call.principal<JWTPrincipal>().subject (Application.kt line 155), a dimension the attacker can mint for free via /v1/auth/register (PublicRoutes.kt lines 35-41, JwtService 90-day TTL). No aggregate limit (per source, global or daily) caps the sum across subjects, and upstream attempts (up to 2 billed provider.complete calls per counted request) are not counted against the budget.
intended_behavior: Operator AI spend should be bounded per real requester and in aggregate. A requester that creates N identities should not get N times the AI budget, and total upstream calls should stay under an operator-configured global ceiling regardless of how many subjects exist.

trace.description: Anonymous registration, gated only by RATE_LIMIT_REGISTER (10/min keyed on origin.remoteHost).
Issues a JWT for a fresh random UUID subject per call.
Each minted token stays valid for 90 days, so identities accumulate.
The AI token bucket (20/min) is keyed only on the JWT subject, so every minted subject gets an independent full budget.
The only accounting wrapper around /v1/ai/{story,evaluate,chat,enrich}.
Each counted request runs up to 2 billed provider.complete calls (corrective retry on invalid output).
POST to the provider's /v1/messages with the operator's x-api-key, retried up to 2 more times on 408/409/429/5xx and network errors.

evidence.description: rateLimiter(limit = config.rateLimitAiPerMinute, refillPeriod = 60.seconds) is the only AI limiter; no global or per-source limiter is registered.
Registration is keyed only on origin.remoteHost at 10/min, so it does not tie identities to an AI budget.
RATE_LIMIT_AI_PER_MINUTE is the only spend knob, and it is per user; no aggregate or spend ceiling exists in config.
Retryable statuses (408/409/429/5xx) are retried up to maxRetries=2 per call, uncounted by the limiter.
validateUser accepts any subject that exists in the store; no account age, activity or per-source binding.

conditions.description: AI_PROVIDER=anthropic with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set (the default is none, under which AI routes return 503).
None beyond self-service anonymous registration; any internet client can mint tokens.

Per-IP registration rate applies when the server sees client IPs directly (compose publishes 8080). Behind a reverse proxy without forwarded-header handling, registration is limited globally at 10/min, which still yields 14,400 new full-budget identities per day. Additional source IPs (e.g. IPv6) multiply the per-IP figure.

Actual monetary loss depends on the operator's provider spend limits outside the repository. If a provider-side cap exists, the same path instead exhausts it and denies AI to all players. Either outcome is a meaningful shared effect; the quota-escape mechanism itself is fully source-proven and does not depend on any unknown deployed control.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous internet client with no prior account, scripting plain HTTP requests from a single source address.
payloads: POST /v1/auth/register {"displayName":"Player A"} (repeated with distinct display names from one source IP)
POST /v1/ai/enrich with header Authorization: Bearer <token_i> and body {"lemma":"apple","meaningTr":"elma","cefr":"B1"} (21 times for each of several tokens)
instructions: Inside tools/sandbox.sh (loopback-only netns, mem 2 GiB, pids 256, CPU 120 s, wall<=300 s), start a Python stub on 127.0.0.1:19011 that answers /v1/messages with a valid enrich JSON and counts hits.

Start com.lexiflow.server.ApplicationKt from /opt/lexiflow-audit-cp with PORT=18090, JWT_SECRET of 40 'x', AI_PROVIDER=anthropic, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=dummy-not-a-real-key, ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:19011, ANTHROPIC_FALLBACKS=off, and no DATABASE_URL.
Register several identities from 127.0.0.1, then send 21 enrich calls with each of 3 tokens, recording statuses and stub hit counts.
execution.observed_result: Independently reproduced by verifier v3-12 (evidence-1.txt): from one source IP, 6 registrations returned 201 x6 (6<10/min register limit). Each of 3 identities got 200 x20 and 429 x1 on /v1/ai/enrich, i.e. 60 billed upstream stub hits from one source in under a minute against a 20/min per-subject limit, using only 3 of the free identities minted that minute. Matches hunter h-spend evidence-1. Hunter h-spend evidence-2 separately showed up to 2 billed provider calls per counted request (corrective retry) and 3 upstream calls per request when the upstream always errors (maxRetries), a bounded contributing multiplier.

remediation.strategy: Add aggregate accounting that new identities cannot reset. Use an operator-configured global AI ceiling and a per-source (trusted client IP) AI budget, layered over the existing per-subject RATE_LIMIT_AI bucket. Count every upstream provider attempt, including the corrective retry and the HTTP retries, against the global ceiling. Do NOT implement the extra limits as nested rateLimit(...) blocks. In Ktor 3.0.3, Route.rateLimit installs the route-scoped RateLimitInterceptors with a single provider name. Core's addAllInterceptors runs a route-scoped interceptor only when findPluginInRoute(call.route) returns that same instance, which is the innermost one, so outer nested limiters are silently skipped. Enforce the extra budgets in one explicit guard instead. Optionally add a persisted daily per-subject quota and a minimum account age or activity before AI access. Make the registration limit configurable and keyed on a trusted forwarded client address behind proxies. Bound or evict the per-source map.

likelihood.reason: Anonymous, scriptable with plain HTTP, needs no special timing, and works from a single source address whenever AI is enabled.

impact.reason: Unbounded growth of operator-paid model spend, or exhaustion of the operator's shared provider quota (single ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) that denies AI to all players. No data compromise or code execution.

confidence.reason: The source path is direct and every trace line and evidence citation was verified against frozen source at 0cf6d494. The quota escape was independently reproduced by the verifier against the real backend jar with a loopback provider stub (60 billed upstream calls from 3 of 6 free identities, one source IP, 20/min per-subject limit). Only the absolute monetary magnitude depends on deployment-side provider limits, and either outcome is a shared effect.

title: Unthrottled full-table leaderboard aggregation can tie up the shared 10-connection pool used by JWT auth and result persistence
description: In Postgres mode, which the shipped docker-compose.yml uses through DATABASE_URL, any registered player can call GET /v1/leaderboard as often and as concurrently as they like. Registration is free and limited only to 10 per minute per IP. The route has no rate limit, no in-flight bound and no cache. Each call first uses one pooled connection for the JWT validateUser -> findUser check. It then takes a second connection and runs a JOIN users + GROUP BY player_id + ORDER BY aggregates over every battle_results row, or every row of one mode, before LIMIT 50. No statement or query timeout is set in code or in compose. The connection is held for the whole query. The pool is a single HikariCP pool with maximumPoolSize=10 and connectionTimeout=10 s. It also serves findUser for every authenticated HTTP request and WebSocket upgrade, BattleManager.saveBattleResults and saveReport. battle_results grows by one row per player per finished room and is never pruned. Attacker-run accounts can grow it: four queued accounts start a room at once, and the room finishes as soon as all of them submit. At 2 messages per round and 20 messages per 10 s per connection, that is about one row per account per second. If per-query time reaches the order of seconds, about 10 concurrent leaderboard calls can hold every connection. Other users' authentication would then wait 10 s and fail with HTTP 500 (the StatusPages Throwable handler). saveBattleResults failures are only logged, so those finished-battle results would be permanently missing from the leaderboard. Whether production query latency reaches that range has not been measured.
claimed_root_cause: The leaderboard route has no per-subject or global rate limit, in-flight bound or cache. Its SQL cost is O(rows in battle_results): the explicit indexes are on mode and player_id, and the implicit ones are the primary key and UNIQUE(room_id, player_id). None of them can serve the aggregate ORDER BY. There is no statement timeout. The query runs on the same single, unpartitioned 10-connection Hikari pool as authentication (findUser) and battle-result and report writes. Attacker-paced read work can therefore starve other principals' authentication and leaderboard integrity.

trace.description: GET /v1/leaderboard. It needs only a valid JWT for an existing user. mode is an optional enum; the absence of mode gives the all-modes, whole-table aggregation.
leaderboardRoutes(store) is mounted at line 197 inside authenticate(AUTH_JWT), with no rateLimit(...) wrapper. RateLimit (lines 152-161) registers only RATE_LIMIT_AI and RATE_LIMIT_REGISTER.

Each authenticated request first calls store.findUser(id), which takes a pooled connection. This applies to the leaderboard calls themselves and to every other user's HTTP or WebSocket authentication.
Calls store.leaderboard(mode, 50) on every request, with no cache or memoisation.
JOIN users + GROUP BY r.player_id, u.display_name + ORDER BY wins, avg_score, games over all matching battle_results rows, then LIMIT. No setQueryTimeout is called and no statement_timeout is set.
dataSource.connection.use(block) on Dispatchers.IO holds one pool connection for the full query duration.
There is one pool, maximumPoolSize = 10, with connectionTimeout = 10_000 at line 173. When it is exhausted, findUser and saveBattleResults wait 10 s and then throw.

evidence.description: install(RateLimit) registers only RATE_LIMIT_AI and RATE_LIMIT_REGISTER. No limiter applies to /v1/leaderboard.

A Throwable from validateUser or findUser (for example Hikari SQLTransientConnectionException after 10 s) is mapped to HTTP 500 'internal'. Authentication for unrelated users fails instead of degrading gracefully.
connectionTimeout = 10_000. No maxLifetime, leak detection or statement or query timeout is configured anywhere in src/ (grep found none).

The explicit battle_results indexes are on mode (line 25) and player_id (line 26). The table also has implicit indexes from PRIMARY KEY(id) and UNIQUE(room_id, player_id) (lines 12 and 22). None of them can serve the aggregate ORDER BY, so each call aggregates every row of the table or of one mode.
store.saveBattleResults runs outside the Mutex, and failures are only logged (lines 284-286). Results lost during pool exhaustion are permanently missing from the leaderboard.

A room finishes as soon as every player has submitted. Four queued attacker accounts start a room at once (tryMatch, line 158), so battle_results grows by about one row per attacker account per second. That rate is bounded only by the per-connection limit of 20 messages per 10 s (Config.kt:22-23). Nothing prunes or caps the table.

The shipped deployment sets DATABASE_URL, so PostgresStore is used. No statement_timeout or Postgres configuration is set, and the server port is published directly with no reverse proxy or rate limiter in front.

blockers: PostgreSQL is not available in the sandbox, and policy forbids installing it. The decisive fact cannot be observed locally: the latency of the exact PostgresStore.leaderboard SQL on PostgreSQL 16 at realistic battle_results sizes, for example 10^6 to 10^7 rows. That latency decides whether about 10 concurrent requests can hold every connection long enough to push other callers past the 10 s connectionTimeout. A SQLite proxy run (artifact v3-13/artifacts/evidence-1.txt) only shows that the same SQL scales linearly with row count: 0.18 s at 100k rows, 0.82 s at 400k and 3.49 s at 1.6M. PostgreSQL's hash aggregation and parallel workers may be much faster, so this is calibration, not proof.

Deployed controls outside the repository are unknown and could prevent the effect: a reverse proxy or gateway with request rate or concurrency limits, a statement_timeout on the Postgres role or database, and the current battle_results row count in production.

Seed dummy rows with generate_series, for example 50k dummy users and 1M and then 5M battle_results rows across the BattleMode values. Run EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the exact PostgresStore.leaderboard SQL, both without the WHERE clause and with WHERE r.mode = 'FIVE_WORD_SENTENCE', and record the execution time. If a run takes 1 s or more, start the backend from /opt/lexiflow-audit-cp in a resource-limited fixture against that DB. Issue exactly 10 concurrent GET /v1/leaderboard requests as 10 of those users, plus one GET /v1/leaderboard with ?mode=INVALID as the 11th user, which needs only findUser and returns 400 when the pool is free. Record whether that 11th request takes about 10 s and returns 500 instead of 400. Stop after that single observation and do not sustain load.

title: Staff-impersonation name block bypassed with Turkish letters and diacritics (Admın, ADMİN, Lexıflow, Ädmin)
description: DisplayNameValidator keeps a reserved set (admin, administrator, moderator, mod, lexiflow, system, support, staff) to stop people impersonating staff, and the backend README says names like 'admin' are blocked. The reserved check only lowercases with Locale.ROOT, de-leets, and then tests each space/_/- separated word for exact membership in the set. It does not apply the Turkish folding that the profanity substring path already uses, it does no NFKD or mark stripping, and it never checks the whole compacted name. As a result, one-letter look-alikes pass. 'Admın' uses dotless ı. 'ADMİN' and 'LEXİFLOW' use dotted capital İ, which lowercases to i + U+0307. 'Lexıflow', 'Moderatör' and 'Sıstem' also pass, as do non-Turkish diacritics ('Ädmin', 'Stäff') and split forms ('Lexi Flow', 'Ad-min'). Each of these is accepted, stored, and issued a 90-day JWT carrying the name. Other players then see the name in match_found (players list), round_result (PlayerResult.displayName) and the public leaderboard (LeaderboardEntry.displayName).
root_cause: In isBlocked (DisplayNameValidator.kt:45-54), the reserved-word test on line 51 is words.any { it in reserved || deLeet(it) in reserved }. Here words are only lowercase(Locale.ROOT) splits (lines 46-47). foldTurkish (line 50, defined at lines 63-64) and the compact form are used only for blockedSubstrings (line 53). No NFKD or combining-mark removal is done anywhere. So any reserved word with a Turkish or accented letter, or split across separators, fails the exact set membership test.
intended_behavior: Before the reserved comparison, a display name is canonicalised: lowercase, de-leet, NFKD with \p{M} removed, Turkish letters folded (ı to i, and so on). The name is rejected if any canonical word is a reserved word, or if the canonical letters-only compact name is a reserved word. Existing blockedWords whole-word behaviour stays unchanged, so harmless names like 'I got it' remain valid.

trace.description: Anonymous route (only rate limited, 10/min per TCP peer) that receives a JSON body {displayName}.
DisplayNameValidator.normalize applies NFC and collapses whitespace. Precomposed İ (U+0130), ı (U+0131), ö and ä are kept as they are.
lowercase(Locale.ROOT) turns 'ADMİN' into 'admi' + U+0307 + 'n' and leaves 'admın' unchanged. There is no fold or mark stripping on this path.

The reserved check is exact set membership of the raw or de-leeted word. 'admın', 'admi̇n', 'lexıflow', 'moderatör', 'sıstem' and 'ädmin' are not members, and neither are the split words 'lexi'/'flow' or 'ad'/'min'.

The user is stored and jwt.issue(user.id, displayName) returns a 90-day token whose name claim is the staff look-alike. BattleManager then broadcasts that name to co-players and records it on the leaderboard.

evidence.description: The reserved set is documented as 'Names that could be used to impersonate staff'.
compactAscii = foldTurkish(compact) is computed, but only the blockedSubstrings check on line 53 uses it. The reserved check on line 51 does not.
foldTurkish maps ı, ğ, ü, ş, ö and ç. It is never applied to the reserved check, and NFKD/mark stripping (needed for İ to i + U+0307 and for ä) exists nowhere in the validator.
The README promises that profanity and names like 'admin' are blocked.
The only reserved-name case is ASCII 'Admin'. There are no Turkish, diacritic or split-word variants.
match_found sends room.players.map { it.displayName } to every player in the room. Lines 266 and 274 carry the name into round_result and the leaderboard record.
LeaderboardEntry.displayName is returned by GET /v1/leaderboard.

conditions.description: None. POST /v1/auth/register is anonymous and rate limited to 10/min per TCP peer.
The impact depends on other players reading a staff-looking name (in match_found, round_result or the leaderboard) as an official account.

execution.attacker_perspective: Anonymous internet client registering a display name that other players will read as a LexiFlow staff, admin or moderator account.
instructions: Run inside tools/sandbox.sh (loopback only). Start java -cp '/opt/lexiflow-audit-cp/*' com.lexiflow.server.ApplicationKt with JWT_SECRET set to 40 dummy 'x' characters, AI_PROVIDER=none and PORT=18081, using the in-memory store (no DATABASE_URL).

Wait for GET /health to answer, then POST /v1/auth/register with Content-Type application/json. Send the ASCII controls first (Admin, admin, LexiFlow, Moderator, System, Support, Staff, Adm1n), then the variants (Admın, ADMİN, Lexıflow, LEXİFLOW, Moderatör, Sıstem, Stäff, Ädmin, 'Destek Admın', 'Lexi Flow', Ad-min, 'LexıFlow Destek').
Pause 61 s after every 10 requests, because the register limit is 10/min per TCP peer and rejected requests also count.
Compare each response's HTTP status, the error code or echoed displayName, and whether a token is present.
execution.observed_result: All ASCII controls (Admin, admin, LexiFlow, Moderator, System, Support, Staff, Adm1n, 'Supp0rt Staff', 'Admin Destek') got HTTP 400 invalid_display_name. Admın (U+0131), ADMİN (U+0130), Lexıflow, LEXİFLOW, Moderatör, Sıstem, Stäff, Ädmin, 'Destek Admın', 'Lexi Flow', Ad-min and 'LexıFlow Destek' each got HTTP 201, with the name echoed back and a token issued (agents/v3-14/artifacts/evidence-1.txt; this matches the hunter's agents/h-wild/artifacts/evidence-2.txt).

remediation.strategy: Canonicalise the name before the reserved comparison only: lowercase(Locale.ROOT), deLeet, NFKD, remove \p{M}, then foldTurkish. Reject when any canonical word, or the canonical letters-only compact name, is a reserved word. Do not route blockedWords through the same folding: canon('göt') = 'got' would reject the currently valid 'I got it', which HttpApiTest asserts is valid. Avoid unbounded substring matching of reserved words, which would reject harmless names such as 'Ecosystem'. Add regression cases for Admın, ADMİN, Lexıflow, Moderatör, Sıstem, Ädmin, 'Lexi Flow' and Ad-min, and keep 'I got it' and 'Klasik Müzik' valid. A mixed-script confusables check (e.g. Cyrillic а) is a possible extra hardening step, not part of this root cause.

likelihood.reason: One anonymous request with a single native Turkish keyboard character is enough. No account, privilege or race is needed. The register rate limit only slows bulk creation.

impact.reason: Cosmetic impersonation: a staff-looking name shown to co-players in battle messages and on the public leaderboard. It grants no privilege and exposes no data, but it defeats the anti-impersonation control the README promises and can support social engineering inside the game.

confidence.reason: Independently reproduced against the real server built from the reviewed commit, inside the sandbox, with ASCII controls rejected and variants accepted. The cause is a single visible check (line 51), and a sibling path in the same function (line 53) already folds Turkish letters.

title: Carbon Fields theme-option text values are echoed unescaped into the public front page (stored XSS where option editors lack unfiltered_html)
description: functions.php registers a Carbon Fields theme_options container with free-text fields hero_title, hero_subtitle, about_title, tokenomics_title, join_title and join_subtitle (functions.php:47,49,54,71,87,89). index.php is the theme's only page template, and on every front-end request it includes the hero, about, tokenomics and join template parts (index.php:14-17). Those parts echo the six values with no escaping: hero.php:15 and 19, about.php:12, tokenomics.php:10, join.php:11 and 14, plus about.php:24 inside an alt="..." attribute, which is rendered only when about_image is set. In the same templates, complex-field sub-values are escaped with esc_html (about.php:40,44; tokenomics.php:21,24,26; join.php:30), esc_url (join.php:23) and esc_attr (join.php:26). On a default single-site install the writer is an administrator who holds unfiltered_html, so no trust boundary is crossed. On WordPress multisite, or with DISALLOW_UNFILTERED_HTML, a sub-site administrator who has manage_options but not unfiltered_html could store markup that runs for every visitor, network super admins included. The theme contains no sanitizer for these fields, and the repository contains nothing showing that Carbon Fields applies kses on save.
claimed_root_cause: Template parts output carbon_get_theme_option() text values with a bare echo instead of esc_html()/esc_attr(). The Carbon Fields text fields are registered with no sanitizer, unlike the customizer settings in inc/customizer.php, which use sanitize_callback.

trace.description: Registers free-text field hero_title in the Carbon Fields theme_options container created at line 45. This container's admin page is the write entrypoint, and Carbon Fields' default capability for it is manage_options (vendor behavior, not in the repository). Sibling text fields: hero_subtitle (49), about_title (54), tokenomics_title (71), join_title (87), join_subtitle (89).

Container::make('theme_options') attaches no sanitize or escape callback to any field. Carbon Fields stores the value. The vendor directory is absent: composer.json requires htmlburger/carbon-fields ^3.6, and functions.php:9 loads vendor/autoload.php.
index.php, the theme's only page template, includes template-parts/hero on every front-end request, then about, tokenomics and join (lines 15-17).

echo carbon_get_theme_option('hero_title') writes the value unescaped into an <h1> on the public page. The same pattern appears at hero.php:19, about.php:12, about.php:24 (alt attribute, rendered only when about_image is set), tokenomics.php:10, join.php:11 and join.php:14.

evidence.description: about_title is echoed raw inside alt="...", so a double quote allows attribute breakout. This output only appears when the about_image option is set (line 21).
Complex-field sub-values in the same template are escaped with esc_html (lines 40 and 44). This shows that output escaping was intended, and that it is missing only for the top-level text options.
Platform links use esc_url (line 23), color_class uses esc_attr (line 26) and name uses esc_html (line 30). In contrast, join_title and join_subtitle at lines 11 and 14 are echoed raw.
tokenomics_title is echoed raw, while the stats sub-fields at lines 21, 24 and 26 use esc_html.
Customizer settings use sanitize_callback (esc_url_raw at lines 16 and 28, sanitize_hex_color at 40). The Carbon Fields options have no equivalent control.
htmlburger/carbon-fields is pinned only to the floating range ^3.6, and no vendor tree is committed. Whether text input passes through kses on save cannot be determined from the repository.

blockers: Deployment fact: is the site WordPress multisite, or does it define DISALLOW_UNFILTERED_HTML, so that someone who can write the Carbon Fields theme options (manage_options by default) lacks unfiltered_html? On a default single site that writer is a fully trusted administrator and no boundary is crossed.

Vendor behavior: the repository does not contain Carbon Fields 3.6.x, so it cannot show whether text-field values are stored without kses filtering for users who lack unfiltered_html. composer.json uses the floating range ^3.6 and no vendor tree is committed.
Local reproduction is not possible in the approved sandbox: PHP, composer, WordPress and a database are unavailable (architecture section 3 and sandbox boundary).

validation_plan.local: In a disposable offline WordPress multisite with this theme and carbon-fields 3.6.x installed through composer, use a dummy sub-site administrator account that lacks unfiltered_html. Set Theme Options > Hero Section > Hero Title to . For the attribute case, set About Title to x" onmouseover="console.log('lexi-xss-marker-2') and set any About Image. Load the sub-site front page as a separate dummy user. Check whether the raw tag or attribute breakout appears in the HTML source and whether the marker logs. Also read the stored option value in wp_options to see whether Carbon Fields applied kses on save. Use only dummy accounts and a throwaway database.
validation_plan.deployment: The owner checks is_multisite() and whether DISALLOW_UNFILTERED_HTML is defined in wp-config.php on the live site, and lists which roles or users hold manage_options without unfiltered_html. This is read-only and requires no changes to content. Whatever the outcome, the source fix is to wrap the six echoes in esc_html() and the alt attribute at about.php:24 in esc_attr().
